tasks.q: Why does a program write data to a file?
a: So the data is still there after the program has stopped running
So the data can be used inside a loop
So the data takes up less memory
So the data is automatically encrypted
tasks.fb: Variables live in RAM and are lost; a file persists on secondary storage.

tasks.q: A quiz program keeps its high scores in variables only. What happens when the program closes?
a: The high scores are lost
The high scores are moved to the hard disk automatically
The high scores become constants
The high scores are output to the screen
tasks.fb: Nothing in RAM survives the program ending unless it has been saved to a file.

tasks.q: Why must a file be opened before it is used?
a: The program needs a link to the file on secondary storage before it can read or write
Files are encrypted until they are opened
Opening a file empties it ready for new data
Opening a file casts its contents to a string
tasks.fb: Open sets up the connection; read and write then use that connection.

tasks.q: In the OCR Exam Reference Language, what does  newFile("log.txt")  do?
a: Creates a new file called log.txt
Opens log.txt ready for reading
Deletes log.txt
Reads the first line of log.txt
tasks.fb: newFile makes the file; openRead or openWrite is then used to work with it.

tasks.q: What does endOfFile() give once every line has been read?
a: True
False
The last line of the file
The number of lines in the file
tasks.fb: The loop carries on while endOfFile() is False, and stops the moment it becomes True.

tasks.q: What does readLine() do each time it is called?
a: Reads the next line of the file
Reads the whole file in one go
Reads the first line again
Writes a new line to the file
tasks.fb: Each call moves one line further on, which is why it works inside a loop.

tasks.q: In Python 3, what happens to data already in a file when it is opened with mode "w"?
a: It is deleted
It is kept, and the new data is added at the end
It is kept, and the new data is added at the start
It is copied into a backup file first
tasks.fb: Mode "w" starts the file again from empty, so use mode "a" when the old data must be kept.

tasks.q: A program uses print() where it should have used write(). What happens to the data?
a: It goes to the screen instead of into the file
It goes into the file as well as onto the screen
It is added to the end of the file
The program stops with a syntax error
tasks.fb: print() is output to the screen; write() is output to a file.

tasks.q: A program must add today's score to a file of past scores. Which Python 3 mode should it use?
tasks.fb: Append mode adds to the end, while write mode would wipe every past score.

tasks.q: Where does appended data go in the file?
a: At the end, after the data that is already there
At the start, before the data that is already there
In place of the data that is already there
Into a second, new file
tasks.fb: That is why a log file read from top to bottom comes out in date order.

tasks.q: What is the main reason a program closes a file after writing to it?
a: To make sure everything still in the buffer is written to the file
To delete the file from the disk
To make the file read-only
To free up space on the hard disk
tasks.fb: Until the file is closed, the last data written may never have left memory.

tasks.q: Which is the correct order of operations on a file?
a: Open, read or write, close
Read or write, open, close
Open, close, read or write
Close, open, read or write
tasks.fb: Nothing can be read or written until the file is open, and nothing is safe until it is closed.

tasks.q: Put these lines into a working program that reads and outputs every line of scores.txt.
tasks.fb: Open, loop while there is still something to read, then close. Forget the close and the file stays locked.

tasks.q: Why does the loop check endOfFile() before it reads a line?
a: Trying to read past the last line would cause an error
It makes the program run faster
It closes the file automatically
It casts each line to an integer
tasks.fb: The check stops the program trying to read a line that is not there.

info.title: RAM is volatile
info.text: RAM loses everything in it when the power goes, which is why it is called volatile. Secondary storage such as an SSD keeps data without power, and that is where files live.

info.title: File paths
info.text: A file name on its own means a file in the same folder as the program. A longer path tells the operating system exactly where to look, which is why a program that works on one computer may not find its file on another.

info.title: CSV files
info.text: A comma separated values file puts one record on each line, with commas between the fields. Reading it line by line and splitting each line at the commas is how most simple data files are loaded.

info.title: Text or binary
info.text: A text file stores characters you could read in a text editor. A binary file stores the raw bytes of an image or a sound, which look like nonsense if you open them as text.

info.title: Logs
info.text: Almost every system you use keeps an append-only log of what happened and when. Because nothing is ever overwritten, the log can be read afterwards to work out what went wrong.

info.title: Lost data
info.text: If a program crashes before closing a file, the last data written can vanish because it never left the buffer. That is one reason programs save as they go rather than only at the very end.

diagrams.title: Reading a file line by line
diagrams.text: The read pointer moves down the file as you read, and what you write is not in the file until it is closed.
